inlines.text: Worker A picks a bucket of blueberries in
Worker B picks a bucket of blueberries in

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write an algebraic expression for the fraction of a bucket of blueberries that could be picked in one hour if A and B worked together.

answer.worked:
In one hour, A picks $\frac{1}{a}$ of a bucket and B picks $\frac{1}{b}$ of a bucket.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Combined fraction}&=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}\\&=\frac{b}{ab}+\frac{a}{ab}\\&=\frac{a+b}{ab}\end{aligned}$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What does the reciprocal of this fraction represent?

answer.short: The time, in hours, for A and B working together to pick one bucket of blueberries.
answer.worked:
$\frac{a+b}{ab}$ represents blueberry buckets per hour.

Its reciprocal, $\frac{ab}{a+b}$, represents hours per bucket of blueberries: the time for A and B working together to pick one bucket.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · example-choice · pf-e2ae243334]
Finding: The equivalent-fraction examples introduce their multipliers without showing how the target denominators determine them.
Breakdown: The algebraic example requires choosing 3b⁵ before multiplying both parts. Showing that multiplier already inserted does not model this decision.
Checked: The preceding definition explains applying the same multiplier, but not choosing it. No earlier teaching supplies the algebraic calculation; the division index law appears afterwards in p4-indices-definition.
Assumes: Students are learning equivalent algebraic fractions. Calculator use does not affect the symbolic decision.
Also affects: p3-equivalent-example-right-example
Proposed repair (add-cue): Add before the respective working: “Required multiplier: 14 ÷ 7 = 2.” and “Required multiplier: 12b⁷ ÷ 4b² = 3b⁵.”
Done when: The examples explicitly derive their multipliers from the original and required denominators.

flags.note:
[Pedagogy review · High priority · opening-review · pf-d71c43a44a]
Finding: The opening topic has no review of multiplying algebraic terms or recognising shared algebraic factors, although its worked examples use both.
Breakdown: Students must recall how powers combine in products and recognise the variable factors available for cancellation while following the new fraction methods.
Checked: All teaching was supplied. No review precedes p3, and p4 states the cancellation method without rehearsing these prior symbolic skills. Finding the highest common factor in one step is unnecessary because the examples cancel factors successively.
Assumes: Algebraic products and recognition of common factors are prior learning from the separately listed algebra and index-law booklets. Calculators do not supply these symbolic decisions.
Also affects: p4-indices-example-a, p4-indices-example-b
Proposed repair (add-review): Insert four short opening items: (a) Simplify 3a × 2b. Answer: 6ab. (b) Simplify 4b² × 3b⁵. Answer: 12b⁷. (c) Which is a factor of both 10a⁵ and 5a²: a² or a⁵? Answer: a². (d) Which is a factor of both 8ab and 2a²: a or a²? Answer: a. Keep the review within one page.
Done when: A short opening review rehearses algebraic multiplication and recognition of shared variable factors.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · example-choice · pf-b588432d91]
Finding: The introductory addition and subtraction examples supply algebraic common denominators without modelling their selection.
Breakdown: Students see equivalent numerators calculated but do not see why shared variable factors appear only once in the lowest common denominator. Multiplying the denominators would also work, concealing this distinction.
Checked: Earlier teaching supplies equivalent fractions with a given target denominator and cancellation. p8 names the lowest common multiple, but its examples and first two guided parts supply it without explaining its algebraic construction.
Assumes: Numerical lowest common multiples are prior knowledge; choosing them for algebraic terms is new in the supplied teaching.
Also affects: p8-example-right-node
Proposed repair (add-cue): Before the examples' supplied denominators, add: “For the lowest common denominator, use the numerical LCM and the highest power of each variable present. For 5 and a², this gives 5a².” Then: “For 3x and 5x, LCM(3, 5) = 15 and the highest power of x is x, so use 15x.”
Done when: The examples connect their original denominators to the chosen common denominators and explain the treatment of shared variable factors.

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · extension · pf-b18d629a4d]
Idea: Use the sum and difference in parts c and d to recover the original fractions.
Why: Combining those results exposes how one original term cancels while the other doubles.
Proposed addition: Append optional parts after p10-q5-o: (p) Add your answers to c and d. Answer: x. (q) Halve your answer to p. Answer: x/2. (r) Subtract your answer to d from your answer to c. Answer: 2x/5. (s) Halve your answer to r. Answer: x/5. (t) Explain why q and s recover the two original fractions in c. Expected explanation: adding the sum and difference cancels the x/5 terms and doubles x/2; subtracting cancels the x/2 terms and doubles x/5.

Finding: The final topic combines fraction operations with cancellation of powers but has no opening review of the latter method.
Breakdown: Both examples require deciding whether surviving powers belong above or below the fraction bar. This prior method must be recalled while multiplication or reciprocal multiplication is also being applied.
Checked: p4 teaches cancellation of powers. The immediately preceding topic practises ordinary fraction operations, cancellation of first powers and products producing powers, but does not rehearse the higher-power cancellation used in p17. These examples also combine methods from earlier topics, so the combined-method review exception applies.
Assumes: Symbolic cancellation is prior learning, and calculators do not perform the required decisions.
Proposed repair (add-review): Insert before p17-information-block: “Simplify: (a) x⁶/x²; (b) y²/y⁵; (c) a³b⁵/(a³b²).” Answers: x⁴; 1/y³; b³. Keep this short review within one page.
Done when: The review rehearses surviving numerator powers, surviving denominator powers and complete cancellation before the combined examples.

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · variation-sequence · pf-3f50fdb738]
Idea: Add a run varying only the numerator exponent to expose where a surviving power appears.
Why: The run crosses from a denominator power through complete cancellation to a numerator power, a central distinction without an existing comparable run.
Proposed addition: Append to p18-q1 under its existing “Simplify” instruction. Add only this instruction: “Predict where the remaining x factor will be before simplifying.” Parts: (g) (x²/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2/x²; (h) (x³/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2/x; (i) (x⁴/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2; (j) (x⁵/3) × (6/x⁴), answer 2x. Follow with unpatterned part (k) (2y³/5) × (15/y⁷), answer 6/y⁴. In g–j only the first numerator exponent changes; coefficients, denominator exponent and operation remain fixed.
